articles.title: Former TOPGUN pilot analyzes Marine Corps pilot's eerie calm after emergency F-18 ejection
articles.summary: Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew Buckley explains the violent forces of ejection and why Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon appeared so calm after his F-18 crash.
articles.body: Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew "Whiz" Buckley told Fox News Digital that the recent crash of a Marine Corps F-18 in Washington state — and the pilot's split-second decision to eject — highlights both the violence of the maneuver and how the ensuing shock can leave an aviator feeling eerily calm. On June 13, 2026, Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon emerged from a wooded area with a bloodied face and walked down the road toward a Yakima County sheriff’s deputy, whose bodycam captured the soldier appearing remarkably composed. "I'm a little frazzled," was about as close as Simon came to expressing fear after his F-18 Hornet crashed into the forest and sparked a small wildfire near Rimrock Lake. Buckley, who flew F-18 Hornets during his 15-year career in the U.S. Navy, said Simon was likely experiencing a combination of shock, an adrenaline letdown and the effects of training that teaches pilots to compartmentalize under pressure. EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE "If anything's going wrong, we focus on the task. Everything else goes away," Buckley told Fox News Digital. "That was the most violent thing that ever happened to that Marine in his entire life." Buckley served as a pilot in the Navy from 1991 to 2006 and said he was fortunate never to have ejected from an aircraft. The experience can have a devastating toll on the human body. "Some folks don't go back to flying status. I mean, you can lose a couple inches in height. Your spine compresses. Some people get shorter," Buckley said. A meta-analysis of more than a dozen studies looking at 1,710 military aircrew ejections found a pooled mortality rate of 10.5%, while 29.8% suffered major injuries. The studies were published between 1971 and 2019. ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE "When you pull that handle, you have two choices: die or maybe live. And I said 'maybe live' because it's incredibly violent. I think the average ejection seat is like 10 to 20 G's of force," Buckley added. "Most folks don't even remember the ejection. They remember pulling the handle and then waking up in their parachute." Buckley said the pilot's body positioning before the ejection is extremely important in preventing potentially life-threatening injuries. For example, if their arm is extended away from their body, the sudden wind blast could cause it to be "ripped out of the socket." There's also a phenomenon called "seat slap," which occurs if the pilot does not have their legs flush with the seat prior to ejecting. "If you look at an ejection seat in a fighter jet, it's rock hard. We're not sitting on a cushion," he said. "If your legs aren't flat on the seat, it could break both of your legs and now you bleed out and die." US NAVY IDENTIFIES SAILOR LOST IN ARABIAN SEA AFTER HELICOPTER'S EMERGENCY WATER LANDING In some instances, pilots who find themselves in trouble have time to slow their aircraft and perform a controlled ejection, which can reduce the forces involved, Buckley said. Based on video of the crash, Simon’s plane was traveling at a high rate of speed before it struck the trees and exploded, likely leaving little opportunity for a controlled ejection. Simon had been performing low-flying maneuvers while spectators on the ground watched, according to KIRO 7. After that, his plane reportedly clipped some power lines, which led to it going down. The Marine Corps has not publicly confirmed that Simon’s F-18 struck power lines before the crash and has said the cause of the mishap remains under investigation. UNITED AIRLINES JET FLEW TOO LOW AND TOO SLOW BEFORE STRIKING LIGHT POLE AND TRUCK NEAR NEWARK AIRPORT: NTSB According to Buckley, this "clearly" wasn't supposed to happen. "We have minimum altitude restrictions. And there ain't no 500-foot trees, right? So I don't know what they were doing. It doesn't sound like from his initial statement that there was anything wrong with the airplane. So that's usually not a good sign," Buckley said. Buckley then speculated about what may have been going through Simon’s mind before the crash. "It looked like a beautiful day. People out on a lake. 'Hey, there's some people down there on the lake. Why don't we go show them what their tax money is [for]? You know, America.' I hope it wasn't something like that," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the third Marine Aircraft Wing, the West Coast-based Marine aviation unit to which Simon’s aircraft was assigned. Buckley said Simon will likely go before a review board that will evaluate his actions surrounding the crash. At the conclusion of the process, the board can recommend what should happen to an aviator’s flight status. If he's found to be at fault, Simon could lose his "wings" or he could be allowed to continue flying, just under what Buckley described as "double secret probation." "I don't know what the board's gonna do, but it'll come out. It should because...this is a $60 to $65 million Hornet. We deserve to know what happened," he added.

articles.title: Syria’s economy poised for improvement after US sanctions removal
articles.summary: Removal of US sanctions offers Syria a chance to fully rejoin the global financial system after years of isolation.
articles.body:
Syria’s removal by the United States from its “state sponsors of terrorism” list clears one of the last major hurdles to the country’s integration into the global financial system, analysts tell Al Jazeera.

On July 8, US President Donald Trump announced he was formally notifying Congress of his intention to rescind Syria’s designation, which had been in place since 1979. A 45-day congressional review period passed on Saturday, and the US completed the formal delisting on Monday .

While Washington had already lifted many of the restrictions preventing transactions with Syrian banks, the “terrorism” designation continued to carry additional financial and trade restrictions, and Syria’s removal will give the country – still struggling to pick itself up after a nearly 14-year war – a badly needed economic boost .

“The momentum is great for this announcement, and it was the last main barrier to banks reconnecting [with the global community],” Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst for Karam Shaar Advisory, a consulting company with a focus on the political economy of the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

Syria was first designated by the US as a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1979 under the presidency of Hafez al-Assad.

The country was originally placed on the list for its support of Palestinian armed groups. Syrian-US relations were later strained when the US invaded Iraq in 2003, just a few years after Hafez died and his son Bashar succeeded him. Washington pulled out of its embassy in Syria in 2012, a year after Syrians rose up against the al-Assad regime, which responded with brutal suppression and violence, leading to war.

During the conflict, Syria became increasingly isolated from the global community as more international sanctions were placed on the regime.

When the al-Assad regime finally collapsed in December 2024, a new government, including members of former rebel groups, took its place. One of its first priorities was trying to reintegrate Syria into the regional and international community by removing the sanctions, which has largely been accomplished .

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the former rebel group he led, were also previously under US sanctions, which have been removed .

While Syria has moved on from its isolation since the fall of al-Assad, its economy remains weak with almost 90 percent of the population living below the poverty line.

“For nearly five decades, Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism resulted in severe restrictions on financing and exports and contributed to significant hesitation and overcompliance among banks and investors who were reluctant to engage with Syria, fearing secondary sanctions,” Obai Kurd Ali, a Syrian expert with the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera.

“People in Syria are suffering from severe poverty and a deteriorating economic situation with decent living standards becoming unaffordable day after day,” he added. “For Syrians, any step that may lead to better living conditions is worth celebrating, and removing [the] designation is not only one such step but also one of the final major actions toward dismantling the complex web of US sanctions that isolated Syria for so long.”

Maresca di Serracapriola said the decision to lift Syria’s designation reduces legal risks for banks working on Syria-related financing or transactions and allows US foreign assistance to Syria.

“The removal of restrictions on US foreign assistance and government contracting has the potential to open additional channels for development and reconstruction support,” he said, adding that “the biggest impact will likely be on financial flows and investment.”

International banks would often cite the designation as a reason against working with banks in Syria.

“The timing of the announcement is important because the Central Bank of Syria reactivated its account at the Federal Reserve Bank in New York in March, and recently, the World Bank has approved a $100m grant for financial sector modernisation in Syria,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.

Ibrahim Kochaji, a Syrian banking and economic expert, called the lifting of the sanctions “a pivotal moment in the trajectory of the national economy” but said it was “not an immediate remedy” for the country’s deep economic struggles.

Kochaji said any resolution to Syria’s issues requires “a long path of reforms and measures” that would be bolstered by stability and sound governance.

Kurd Ali agreed. “The transitional government must seize this opportunity to put its own house in order,” he said. “Good governance, transparency, robust anticorruption measures and meaningful judicial reform are essential to regain investors’ confidence and ensure that investment contributes to a sustainable and inclusive recovery that puts people’s priorities at its heart.”

The fall of the al-Assad regime was met with jubilation across Syria. And many Syrians still speak about the improvements to their day-to-day lives since the regime’s demise.

But increasingly, Syrians are expressing frustration at the soaring cost of energy and the stuttering local economy.

Kochaji said the removal of sanctions would impact Syrians daily lives but the impact may not be as immediate as some may hope.

“The realistic answer is that the impact will be gradual, but it can become tangible if the government manages the transition wisely,” he said, adding that if managed correctly, production and transportation costs could decrease and new job opportunities could develop, among other potential benefits.

While many of the main economic barriers have been removed, analysts said they believe Syria’s banking sector is not guaranteed to automatically rebound.

“International banks and investors will still look at Syria’s antimoney-laundering and counter-financing of terrorism framework and overall risk environment, also general governance and political stability,” Maresca di Serracapriola said. “So that will not necessarily shift the picture entirely with respect to banking.”

WorldTrips is a top-rated travel insurance provider that offers flexible policy options and strong financial stability. Learn more about its coverage limits, plan costs, and add-ons in our WorldTrips travel insurance review.

What does WorldTrips travel insurance cover?

This is a general overview of the different types of coverage you can expect from WorldTrips.

Trip cancellation: Covers up to the trip cost if you cancel for a covered reason.

Trip interruption: Often covers more than the trip cost if you interrupt your travels for a covered reason.

Travel delay: Provides up to a set limit per day (with a maximum overall limit) for covered travel delays.

Missed connection: Provides up to a certain amount if you miss a travel connection for a covered reason.

Airline reissue or cancellation fees: Provides up to a certain amount to help cover airline reissue or cancellation fees.

Reinstate frequent traveler awards: Helps cover any fees for reinstating frequent traveler awards, points, or miles.

Single occupancy coverage: Helps cover increased travel costs if a travel companion cancels their trip.

Travel assistance services: Provides 24/7 support for emergency travel arrangements, translator referrals, legal referrals, and more.

Accidental death and dismemberment: Provides up to a certain amount for covered situations involving accidental death and dismemberment.

Emergency accident and sickness medical expense: Covers emergency medical care while traveling.

Dental expense: Covers emergency dental expenses while traveling.

Medical evacuation and repatriation of remains: Covers necessary medical evacuation and repatriation expenses.

Baggage damage or loss: Provides up to a specified amount for covered losses when your baggage is lost, damaged, or stolen.

Baggage delay: Provides up to a certain amount for reasonable expenses when experiencing covered baggage delays.

Cancel for any reason (CFAR): With CFAR coverage, you can receive up to 75% of your trip costs back if you cancel due to a non-covered reason.

Adventure sports: Extends your insurance coverage to also include activities such as bungee jumping, hang gliding, safaris, and more.

Rental car damage and theft: Adds a collision damage waiver and coverage for rental vehicle theft.

Medical evacuation: Doubles your medical evacuation coverage and provides you with the option to choose which hospital you would like to be evacuated to.

Pet care: Adds trip cancellation coverage to your policy if a traveling pet companion becomes critically ill or dies during the trip.

Adventure sports (unless you choose the optional upgrade)

Preexisting medical conditions (unless you have the waiver)

Traveling against the advice of a physician

articles.body:
The Secret Service on Tuesday said it was aware of a video threatening President Trump’s son, Barron, being circulated by Iranian state media.

Clips suggest that Iran’s leaders are tracking Barron’s whereabouts and offering a $10 million reward to those who can provide insight into his location, according to reports from ABC News .

“The U.S. Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees,” Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said in a statement to NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

“Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence,” Herring added.

In previous instances, Iran has circulated videos and statements threatening to kill the president and his family members. The stakes have heightened as the war in Iran nears the six-month mark with no clear end in sight.

The Trump administration has waged both military and economic war on Tehran and pushed its leaders to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic.

Iran has refused but agreed to work with Oman to open two pathways through the critical waterway for a fee.

Since the U.S. and Israel first struck Iran in February, its leaders have been seeking revenge for the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the strikes.

Iran held a weeklong national ceremony in July to commemorate Khamenei’s life while appointing his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, to serve in his place.

Mojtaba Khamenei was reportedly injured in U.S.-Israeli strikes and has remained absent from direct negotiations with U.S. envoys.

The U.S. and Iran reached a brief ceasefire on June 17 following Pakistan-mediated talks.

President Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum of understanding enshrining a 14-point agreement that halted military operations and aimed to reopen the strait.

However, the fragile ceasefire began to break down in early July after renewed vessel attacks in the strait, and the 60-day agreement ultimately expired last week.

articles.title: NYC mom survives neck-slash attack on hiking trip in Arizona: 'I can’t die like this'
articles.summary: Ring camera footage captures New York City mother Alexis Rowan fighting for her life after a stranger slashed her neck on an Arizona birthday hike.
articles.body: A birthday hiking trip of a lifetime wound up being a death-defying fight for her life for a New York City mother of two, leaving her neck slashed, her hand stabbed, as well as physical and emotional scars that left 13 stitches and a nightmare that will never be forgotten. Alexis Rowan, 27, survived the northern Arizona mountain-hike attack only because of screams that were heard by a woman in a nearby home, forcing the suspect to flee, harrowing doorbell camera footage showed. "I was like, oh my God, my neck: I can't die like this, this is not the way," Alexis Rowan told WABC after returning to New York City after last week's ordeal on a tourist mountain hike in Arizona. "I have my kids to go home to." NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' Graphic photos shared by the New York Post showed the deep slash left on her neck and the 10 stitches that closed it, along with three more from being stabbed in the hand. She never wants "to look at another mountain again," she told the Post, while the lasting scar will remind her of the horror with every look in the mirror. On the Wednesday, Aug. 19, hike at the Havasupai Indian Reservation – just one day after her 27th birthday – Alexis was left briefly behind a friend when the suspect approached. The suspect, identified as Taylor Nardo Paya, 29, is a Havasupai tribe member with a rap sheet that included a guilty plea to assault, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL "It was the first person that I've seen in the village, and I said, 'Hey, excuse me, is that the gift shop?'" Rowan told WABC in one of the few interviews she granted. Fox News Digital reached out to her and her mother for an interview, but they have yet to respond. "I kept walking, I went to go in and that's when he just came up from behind," she continued, "and as soon as I felt my neck, I'm like, 'oh my God, I'm going to die.'" Footage showed Rowan fighting for her life as she was dragged by the hair from the ground – with her screams finally bringing a woman to open the door and causing the suspect to flee. The video obtained by Fox News Digital did not have the sound of the screams, but they were key to the suspect fleeing, according to reports. REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF COLLEGE STUDENT’S MURDER WAS KNOWN ‘THREAT’ AFTER PRIOR ARREST: VICTIM’S MOM "I'm just so grateful for the woman that opened the door that heard her screams; it's something you can never unhear," Tricia Rowan, Alexis' mother, told WABC of the "angel sent from heaven" woman who opened the door to help. "She's a fighter. She fought to make sure she's coming home to her babies, and she's my baby. So I'm so glad she made it, Tricia Rowan said. "He picked the wrong one. My daughter is a fighter, she is a warrior. She wasn’t going to take it." SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS Alexis Rowan told the Post she was "mentally aware" of the "danger" after her initial interaction with Paya. "My gut instinct was like, ‘This is not OK. I’m not OK,’" she said, adding that the "next person may not be as strong, may not be prepared mentally that someone is going to attack them or able to put them in danger." Reservation police located Paya the following day by pinging Rowan’s phone, which prosecutors say he allegedly stole after it fell from one of her backpacks. WOMAN ALLEGEDLY CHOKED SUBWAY RIDER, YELLED ANTISEMITIC REMARKS IN ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO: POLICE He was arrested and later taken into federal custody because the alleged attack occurred on tribal land, according to reports. Video obtained by Fox News Digital showed Paya being cuffed and taken away on a golf cart by federal police before another video showed him in an orange jumpsuit being perp-walked to a helicopter. Paya faces a federal assault with a deadly weapon charge, according to FOX 10. Court records show Paya pleaded guilty in 2016 to robbing and assaulting another woman in a 2015 attack, for which he received a five-year prison sentence and was ordered to undergo sex offender treatment and counseling. FIVE PLEAD GUILTY TO CHARGES IN BRUTAL CINCINNATI BEATDOWN THAT WENT VIRAL LAST SUMMER The victim's mother wants to see the perpetrator locked up indefinitely. "People are evil," she told the Post, calling him "a threat to society" and someone "you cannot rehabilitate." articles.title: Dolly Parton, singer-songwriter, 1946-2026
articles.summary: Dolly Parton was at once larger than life and down to earth. The Nashville star, who has died aged 80, was a vision of fabulous folksiness with...
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was at once larger than life and down to earth. The Nashville star, who has died aged 80, was a vision of fabulous folksiness with her blonde wigs, rhinestones and dazzling smile. She wrote songs in industrial quantities, about 3,000 in her estimation, but performed them with a very human wit and warmth. With more than 100mn record sales to her name and a renown stretching far beyond the boundaries of her genre, she ranks among the greatest artists in the history of country music.

She was born in rural Tennessee in 1946, at the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains. Her father was a sharecropper who later became a tobacco farmer. Her mother had 12 children, including Parton, by the age of 35. It was an impoverished upbringing. According to Parton, her penniless father paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. "I have often joked that I have been raking in the dough ever since," she wrote in her autobiography, Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business .

There was neither self-pity nor selfishness in her passage from rags to riches. She sang about being mocked by schoolmates for wearing a coat made from scraps of fabric in "Coat of Many Colors". "I couldn't understand it, for I felt I was rich," Parton sang in the 1971 signature song. "And I told them of the love my momma sewed in every stitch." At this point in the song, a key change lifts us up too.

She could dole out schmaltz with the best of them, although she was a sophisticated singer and songwriter too. Drawn to music from a young age, she was brought up amid the music of church and family gatherings rather than records or radio. After graduating from high school, she left home for Nashville in 1964. Another autobiographical song, "The Letter", evokes the small-town girl's first weeks in Music City, singing on morning television shows and writing hits for other acts.

Her first country hit as a recording artist came in 1967 with the single "Dumb Blonde". "This dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool," she sang. It was penned by another Nashville songwriter, but the mix of self-mockery and defiance was typical of Parton . Country music's tradition of strong womanhood allowed a certain degree of challenge to its even more powerful culture of sexism. Parton was audacious yet also astute in testing the limits that she faced.

Initially, her extravagantly quivering voice was divisive. "I just don't think the girl can sing," a record executive told Nashville veteran Porter Wagoner when he proposed teaming with Parton as a duo in 1967. Wagoner insisted, and the partnership was a success. It provided the platform for her solo career to blossom in the early 1970s with hits such as "Coat of Many Colors".

articles.title: 'Shocking' book about Putin's private life wins French literary prize
articles.summary: A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin's rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French litera...
articles.body:
A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin's rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French literary prize on Tuesday.

The book, titled "The Tsar in Propria Persona: How Vladimir Putin Deceived Us All", draws on more than two decades of investigative reporting by journalists Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin.

The work won a newly established literary award called the Prix Strasbourg awarded by EBRA, France's largest regional newspaper group, and its parent company, Credit Mutuel Alliance Federale.

The book is due to be published in France next month.

It reads "like a spy novel", the jury said, describing the book as a "fascinating and shocking work about a figure who is himself fascinating and shocking".

"It is the result of several hundred interviews with witnesses, some of whom later disappeared under tragic circumstances."

Badanin is the founder and editor-in-chief of Proekt, an investigative media outlet created in 2018.

Both Badanin and Rubin, his deputy at Proekt, live in the United States after coming under pressure in Russia.

Badanin said the authors wanted foreigners to read the book and learn "actual facts" about Putin and the system he had built.

"The message we wanted to convey with this book is as follows: there is no need to invent anything about Putin. Instead, learn how things really are. That is horrifying enough," he told AFP.

"Only a genuine understanding of the facts can help us make sound assessments, respond effectively, and plan for the future of relations between nations."

When the book's Russian edition was published last year, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) said that Badanin and Rubin broke a Kremlin-imposed taboo about Putin's private life "at great personal risk".

The book "contrasts the official image of the Russian president, now in his 26th year in power, as a leading defender of traditional values against Western decadence with the reality of his private life -- where extramarital affairs, nepotism, and connections to organised crime reign".

Launched in 2026, the prize seeks to distinguish itself through its substantial endowment, with 20,000 euros ($23,000) awarded to the overall winner and 55,000 euros distributed across all categories.

Other prize winners include Haitian author Thelyson Orelien and French journalist Marion Dubreuil.

articles.title: Democrats push Rubio on Board of Peace ‘slush fund’ for Trump
articles.summary: House Democrats are applying new scrutiny on President Trump’s Board of Peace, demanding answers on how his inner circle is using American tax dollars for a “slush fund” and planning to profit off plans to rebuild the Gaza Strip. The Trump administration was forced to halt the transfer of $50 million to the board in…
articles.body:
House Democrats are applying new scrutiny on President Trump’s Board of Peace, demanding answers on how his inner circle is using American tax dollars for a “slush fund” and planning to profit off plans to rebuild the Gaza Strip.

The Trump administration was forced to halt the transfer of $50 million to the board in July, in the face of pushback from lawmakers who said the State Department could not answer basic questions about the board’s structure, oversight of the funds, and whether Trump could use the funds to compensate himself.

Those questions form the basis of a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday and obtained exclusively by The Hill. The letter also signals that Democrats will open an investigation into Trump’s Board of Peace if they take the majority in the House after the November midterm elections, in which case they would gain subpoena power.

Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking members of the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees, respectively, call for Rubio to answer basic questions about the board’s structure, funding and oversight, nine months after its creation.

“The fact that the Trump Administration, with your help, is attempting to transfer taxpayer dollars to the Board of Peace, an opaque organization primed for corruption, raises serious concerns that public funds could be once again misused by the President and his family and friends,” the lawmakers wrote.

Trump created the Board of Peace in October as part of a plan to end the devastating war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip, appointing himself as “chairman for life” with apparent unilateral control over the board’s decisions and how money is spent on reconstruction — even beyond his presidency.

The United Nations Security Council endorsed the board until 2027. But in January, Trump expanded the board’s mission to tackle conflict around the world, setting it up to outlive the Security Council deadline. The president solicited billion-dollar pledges from countries in exchange for lifetime membership and promised an initial pledge of $10 billion from the U.S. government.

A Board of Peace official earlier told The Hill that hundreds of millions of dollars have been collected to finance the Gaza peace plan. The Financial Times reported in May that donors preferred placing funds in a bank account managed by J.P. Morgan , rather than the account set up at the World Bank.

Democrats and other critics say there are no clear answers on who is auditing and conducting oversight of the J.P. Morgan account.

On July 29, the State Department notified Congress it was rescinding $50 million in funding it was sending to the Board of Peace from its budget for international organizations and programs.

The notification followed intense pressure from Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, a congressional aide told The Hill. The Board of Peace did not respond to a letter Shaheen sent them in June raising questions about funds, but it has started briefing committee staff, the congressional aide said.

Raskin and Meeks’s letter adds to that pressure. The lawmakers argue that basic questions on whether the Board of Peace is a public or private entity, a U.S. organization or international, or “even a false entity altogether” are unanswered.

“Can anyone assure Congress that billions of dollars from U.S. taxpayers and foreign governments will not be flowing into the pockets of President Trump, members of his family, corrupt and incompetent contractors or business partners, or political allies and foot soldiers of the President?” the lawmakers wrote.

Raskin and Meeks also argue that Trump’s executive order establishing the Board of Peace as a “public international organization” — which would protect it from lawsuits and certain searches from federal law enforcement — is without merit.

A Board of Peace official earlier told The Hill that the board “is an international organization established under international law. Its legal status and mandate derive from the foundational arrangements establishing it and the consent of its participating members.”

But Raskin and Meeks said that such an organization must be established under a treaty or an act of Congress.

“The Board of Peace was created out of thin air and whole cloth by the President, without any input from Congress about any aspect of its operation,” they wrote.

The lawmakers argue that Board of Peace members have been “explicit” about their intention to use it for “private profit-making purposes,” pointing to statements by Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and a board member, advertising “amazing investment opportunities” when promoting the administration’s Gaza plan to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.

And Raskin further points out that the administration’s goal to trademark Board of Peace earlier this year served as a flashing red light for “backroom deals and procedural illegitimacy.”

Earlier this year, in a move that Raskin described as “almost certainly illegal,” the director of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, John Squires, applied for trademarks on behalf of the board. Squires told Raskin at a Judiciary hearing in March that he filed the trademark to preserve access to the Board of Peace website address in his authority as adviser to the president.

“After Judiciary Committee Democrats demanded information on this trademark application in three oversight letters to Director Squires, he abruptly abandoned the applications but failed to respond to any of our letters or provide information as to who directed him to apply for this trademark for the Board in the first place,” Raskin and Meeks wrote.

The lawmakers gave Rubio a Sept. 8 deadline to answer more than a dozen questions on who manages the Board of Peace, the decisionmaking process, who has the authority to make financial decisions, staffing, what bank accounts are being used and how it’s being overseen, among other questions.

“We will work with you to guarantee the American people full transparency about how their tax dollars are being funneled to — and spent by — this organization never established or authorized by Congress but now poised to receive substantial public funding from the State Department under your direction,” they wrote.

There’s been little progress in finally ending the conflict between Israel and Hamas in Gaza, the narrow seaside territory divided under majority Israeli control but with nearly 2 million Palestinians living under Hamas control. Thousands are displaced, living in bare-bones temporary shelters of tarps or damaged buildings and facing shortages of water, food and medicine.

Last month, the Board of Peace proposed a roadmap to disarm Hamas, and it is pushing Israel to accept the proposal. However, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shown little interest in finding common ground with Hamas as he fights for his political survival in upcoming elections.

The board is working toward developing a “pilot zone” where tens of thousands of Palestinians could move into reconstructed neighborhoods in southern Gaza free of Hamas control.

articles.title: Nearly 6-foot cobra hiding under kitchen sends India family rushing to safety
articles.summary: Frightened residents may try to trap or kill it instead of calling trained professionals.
articles.body:
A nearly six-foot cobra hiding beneath a kitchen in India sent one family rushing to safety after hissing and movement inside the home revealed a dangerous surprise.

As The Live Nagpur reported , the rescue ended without injury to either the residents or the snake, but the incident showed how quickly a wildlife encounter can become a major safety concern.

At around 2 p.m. on Aug. 11, 2026, the Songade family left their home in Gayatri Colony and alerted neighbors after tracing hissing and movement in the kitchen to a cobra concealed beneath the kitchen area, the publication said.

As neighbors gathered outside, Shubham G.R., president of Wild Animals and Nature Helping Society, was called to the scene. He captured the cobra from the kitchen and released it into the wild, according to TLN.

A venomous cobra inside a home poses a serious risk, especially in a confined indoor space. In India, these types of events crop up from time to time, and it can be alarming for locals.

While it is unclear exactly why this cobra entered the house, situations like this can be linked in part to human activity.

As homes, roads, and neighborhoods expand into or alongside wildlife habitat, animals and people are pushed into closer contact. Even common features around homes, including dark corners, stored belongings, food scraps, and rodents, can make residential spaces appealing hiding spots for snakes.

The BBC has reported that human expansion into natural spaces can increase dangerous encounters with wild animals, creating risks for both residents and animals trying to navigate altered environments.

A cobra in a kitchen can drive a family from their home and cause panic throughout a neighborhood. The situation can also turn deadly for the snake, as frightened residents may try to trap or kill it instead of calling trained professionals.

Instead of trying to deal with the cobra themselves, TLN noted the family kept away from it, alerted others, and sought help from a trained rescuer.

Wildlife rescuers say that is the right response when a snake is found indoors. People should keep their distance, make sure children and pets stay away from the area, and contact an authorized wildlife rescue team or trained snake rescuer as quickly as possible.

Reducing the chances of similar encounters can involve keeping homes and nearby areas clean, limiting places where snakes can hide, and addressing conditions that attract prey animals such as rodents.

Those steps may not eliminate the risk entirely, particularly in places close to wildlife habitat, but they can help reduce the odds of a frightening encounter inside the home.

Fortunately, in this case, the family was unharmed, and the cobra was removed safely, avoiding a much worse outcome.
